Cliff and I have kids about the same age, and this is the question every parent is facing now - how should we educate our kids when AI can do almost anything ?

Cliff: "Increasingly, I'm of the view that we should spend a bunch of time with kids basically separated from these models, teaching them basic skills that we think are important. 

The more intelligence you have, which would be sorts of education, the better you are at communicating with a model and telling a model what you want.

Yes, model can do it, but you need to know it so that you can tell the model what to do.

And then on the flip side, some English teacher is like, 'I don't like models because the kids just cheat on their Shakespeare essays.' 

I'm like, 'You're not being ambitious enough.' 

If the kids are cheating on a Shakespeare essay, give them something 100 times harder and more ambitious, and have them use models to their fullest extent.

Have them bring the work product back and then make sure that they didn’t just give a prompt to the model.

Make sure they own it. Ask them why it's like this. Force them to justify it.

Those kids need to be good at using them, and they also just need to be taught that they can do anything."

This month @Deloitte published “Five Trends Shaping Marketing in 2026”.

Here’s the TL;DR ↓

1. Budget pressure is rising: shorter horizons, tighter spend, more CFO scrutiny, and tougher ROI demands.

2. Consumers are more selective and cutting non-essentials, but will still pay more when the value feels clear.

3. Customer experience is becoming a bigger differentiator, and discovery is shifting beyond search to social, creators, communities, and recommendations.

4. AI can lower content costs, speed production, and improve personalisation – but trust is shaky.

5. Most firms are investing more in AI, yet big returns from agentic AI are still rare. Value often takes years and depends on systems, governance, and operating model – not tools alone.

My reading:

2026 is probably the year when everything that used to work in marketing suddenly stopped working – attribution broke, and ROAS started falling across key acquisition channels.

If I had to share my 5 marketing projections for 2027, they’d be:

• More experimentation with AI optimisation; a race for recommendations and citations

• A marketing-budget crisis – and increased demand for evidence-based marketing

• A new rise of guerrilla and situational marketing

• Trust/brand become economic assets

• AI becomes part of marketing workflows; teams that ignore AI underperform and get fired

What are yours?

Spot gold was $4,073.40/oz, up 0.35% on Kitco’s daily comparison, at 4:06 p.m. New York time.

That puts gold comfortably above the roughly $4,030 level quoted in the earlier update. Encouraging resilience following the decision, although one afternoon’s recovery needs follow-through.

🥈 SILVER: Recovers above $54

Spot silver was $54.43/oz, up 0.26%, around 4:04 p.m. New York time, after trading as low as $53.18 during the session.

The gold/silver ratio is approximately 74.8. Silver has recovered, but I’m watching whether it can reclaim $55 and sustain the move.

🟠 COPPER: Above $14,500

The LME’s latest published three-month closing price is $14,621/t. Its closing table also shows aluminium at $3,250/t and tin at $54,010/t.

Copper has moved above the $14,500 level highlighted earlier. These are LME closing benchmarks, established before the Fed announcement—not a measure of the post-decision reaction.

☢️ URANIUM: Contracting remains the signal

The latest verified industry briefing I’m using remains October 27: physical spot at $89.85/lb for the previous Friday and October’s long-term indicator at $97/lb.

My take: gold and silver’s recovery is encouraging despite the Fed’s continued inflation concerns. Copper’s elevated pricing and stronger uranium contracting add separate reasons to keep watching the sector.

The next test is whether precious metals hold these gains as markets digest the decision and the next inflation data.

WHY ON EARTH ARE WE TALKING ABOUT THE DEFAULT RISK OF ANTHROPIC? 

A prediction market is taking real money on an Anthropic bankruptcy by 2028. Look at the balance sheet before you take the other side. Anthropic holds $112bn of cash and cash equivalents plus $19bn of short-term investments, $132bn in all. That is the third-largest pile in corporate America, behind Berkshire and Alphabet, ahead of Amazon, SpaceX, Meta and Microsoft.

Two things about that cash that nobody has priced. First, it earns. $132bn at a 4% bill yield is roughly $5bn a year of interest income, and that is before anyone counts a token of revenue. The company turned an operating profit of $974m in Q2. Add the yield on the cash and the cash-flow-positive story is not even close; it was already there, and the income on the pile was never part of the calculation.

Second, the burn. Over its entire lifetime Anthropic has burned under $13bn of cash, less than a tenth of what it holds today, and the worst year was 2025. So let me make the burn timeline, in a risk scenario, for the people on the other side of that contract.

At the Q2 run-rate the pile does not fall at all. At $25bn a year, twice the worst year so far, the cash lasts to 2031. At $50bn a year, four times the worst year, it lasts to 2029. At $100bn a year, the entire compute bill with zero revenue, it lasts past 2027.

And in all of this, we haven't even considered that they are about to raise even MORE cash.. The credit/default risk panic around AI is absolutely hysterical.

team clearly knows who their target customers are and has shown that there is a clear demand for their product (discounted, cheap inference for new builders). much more work to do on both the demand and supply side imo, but so far so good

robinhood:0xaa07a0e9209e16ac99708c3ec70159c6ef3128a3 - one of the revenue generators on RH. Inference demand is still climbing, with real usage from non-crypto users buying discounted inference via card. Revenue cooled a bit after the initial spike, but the product shows sticky demand. A large portion of revenue comes from trading fees on the underlying token, so this piece is market-condition dependent and should pick up as activity does. Team has partnered with NEAR and Phala for private inference and is expanding supply.

they’re also building an agentic launchpad on Mosh where projects pair against ORBIO and fees route into the agent’s stake + CREDIT so agents can fund their own inference. The team already knows how to supply and route demand on RH and the launchpad is the next layer that turns ORBIO into the base asset funding agent runtimes.

$BUN - sits at the intersection of launchpad infra × agenticFi × revenue × ownership. Mosh locks ~70% of supply in non-custodial vaults controlled by AI agents that market-make (they can trade but can’t withdraw). BUN was the first token launched this way and already has agents accumulating ETH from activity. Teams like Orbio are using it for their own agentic launchpads.

as agents market-make those pairs they accumulate more of the underlying token, which then further supports liquidity. This reflexivity flywheel compounds with every additional launch and becomes more obvious when on-chain liquidity conditions improve.
